candidates.quote: A small daily task, if it be really daily, will beat the labours of a spasmodic Hercules. It is the tortoise which always catches the hare.
candidates.author: Anthony Trollope
candidates.locator: Chapter VII (Doctor Thorne, The Bertrams, The West Indies and the Spanish Main), in the paragraph on his working diary; Blackwood, 1883; full text at Project Gutenberg #5978, where the two sentences are consecutive
candidates.whyThisMonth: The whole month in one sentence from the most methodical novelist in English: the small task done every day beats the heroic burst, and the day’s small task is within reach at six.

candidates.quote: Great works are performed not by strength, but perseverance; yonder palace was raised by single stones, yet you see its height and spaciousness. He that shall walk with vigour three hours a day, will pass in seven years a space equal to the circumference of the globe.
candidates.author: Samuel Johnson
candidates.work: The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia
candidates.locator: Chapter XIII (Rasselas discovers the means of escape), said as the two dig their way out of the Happy Valley; Project Gutenberg #652, where the speaker is given as ‘his companion’, who is Imlac
candidates.speaker: Imlac, to Prince Rasselas
candidates.whyThisMonth: It turns a daunting piece of work into arithmetic: single stones, three hours a day, and the globe is walked round, which is the right sum to do before the day starts.

candidates.quote: Be moderate in thy sleep; for he who does not rise early does not get the benefit of the day; and remember, Sancho, diligence is the mother of good fortune, and indolence, its opposite, never yet attained the object of an honest ambition.
candidates.author: Miguel de Cervantes
candidates.locator: Part II, chapter 43 (Of the second set of counsels Don Quixote gave Sancho Panza); Project Gutenberg #996. The proverb alone also stands in Part I, chapter 46
candidates.speaker: Don Quixote, to Sancho Panza
candidates.whyThisMonth: Advice written for the reader who is already up: the knight’s counsel to a new governor is that the early riser gets the day and diligence makes the luck.

candidates.quote: But then I have always supposed it to be my own fault—because I would not take the trouble of practising.
candidates.author: Jane Austen
candidates.locator: Chapter 31 (Volume II, chapter 8), at the pianoforte at Rosings, answering Darcy; Project Gutenberg #1342. The first edition prints a dash after fault
candidates.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet, to Mr Darcy
candidates.whyThisMonth: Elizabeth refuses the excuse of talent: her fingers are as capable as anyone’s and the only thing missing is the practice, which is an honest thing to admit early in the day.

candidates.quote: In the conduct of life, habits count for more than maxims, because habit is a living maxim, becomes flesh and instinct. To reform one’s maxims is nothing: it is but to change the title of the book. To learn new habits is everything, for it is to reach the substance of life. Life is but a tissue of habits.
candidates.author: Henri-Frédéric Amiel
candidates.work: Amiel’s Journal: The Journal Intime of Henri-Frédéric Amiel
candidates.locator: Undated entry printed between those of 30 December 1850 and 17 February 1851; Macmillan, 1885; Project Gutenberg #8545, the whole paragraph
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month’s theme stated by a diarist to himself: resolutions only retitle the book, and the day is changed by the habit actually practised in it.

candidates.quote: Looking back, I imagine I was always writing. Twaddle it was, too. But better far write twaddle or anything, anything, than nothing at all.
candidates.author: Katherine Mansfield
candidates.locator: Entry headed July 1922, Sierre, the last lines before the editor’s note on her return to London; ed. J. Middleton Murry (Knopf, 1927), p. 245, read in the archive.org scan journalofkatheri00mans. The 1927 text has a comma after was
candidates.whyThisMonth: Permission to begin badly: a writer who held herself to the hardest standard tells her own notebook that a poor page is worth more than a blank one.

candidates.quote: How vain it is to sit down to write when you have not stood up to live!
candidates.author: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.locator: Entry of 19 August 1851; The Writings of Henry David Thoreau, Journal II, ed. Bradford Torrey (Houghton Mifflin, 1906); Project Gutenberg #59031. The next sentence is on his legs moving and his thoughts beginning to flow
candidates.whyThisMonth: A reminder that the desk is the second discipline and the walk the first: it sends the reader out to move before sitting down to the work.

candidates.quote: Just as iron rusts unless it is used, and water putrifies or, in cold, turns to ice, so our intellect spoils unless it is kept in use.
candidates.author: Leonardo da Vinci
candidates.work: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci (The Literary Works of Leonardo da Vinci)
candidates.locator: Richter no. 1177, section XIX, Philosophical Maxims. Morals. Polemics and Speculations; London, 1883; Project Gutenberg #5000, which spells putrifies so. Often quoted in the later wording ‘Iron rusts from disuse’, which is not this edition’s
candidates.whyThisMonth: A notebook maxim that makes daily use a matter of upkeep rather than ambition: the mind, like iron and water, keeps only by being worked.
candidates.translator: Jean Paul Richter’s edition, 1883, whose preface credits the English mainly to Mrs R. C. Bell
candidates.year: c. 1490 to 1519, in the notebooks; first printed 1883

candidates.quote: What is needed is constant work, day and night, constant reading, study, will. … Every hour is precious for it.
candidates.author: Anton Chekhov
candidates.work: Letters of Anton Chekhov to His Family and Friends
candidates.locator: Letter to his brother Nikolay, Moscow, 1886 (the letter on what cultured people are like), near the close; Chatto and Windus, 1920; Project Gutenberg #6408. Garnett prints will.... and it.... with her own ellipses; the mark of omission here is hers
candidates.whyThisMonth: An older brother’s whole programme for becoming someone, with no mention of talent: work, reading, study and will, and the hour in hand counted as precious.

candidates.quote: Life is perhaps eternal, and therefore work is eternal. If this is so, let us do our day’s work bravely.
candidates.author: George Sand
candidates.locator: Letter CCCII, to Gustave Flaubert, Nohant, 12 January 1876; Boni and Liveright, 1921; Project Gutenberg #5115
candidates.whyThisMonth: At seventy-one she answers her friend’s despair with a plain order for the morning: whatever else is true, there is the day’s work, and it can be done bravely.

candidates.quote: The Habits of a vigorous mind are formed in contending with difficulties. All History will convince you of this, and that wisdom and penetration are the fruits of experience, not the Lessons of retirement and leisure.
candidates.author: Abigail Adams
candidates.work: Letter to John Quincy Adams, 19 January 1780
candidates.locator: Adams Family Correspondence, vol. 3, ed. L. H. Butterfield and Marc Friedlaender (Harvard University Press, 1973), p. 268, in her own capitals; Massachusetts Historical Society digital edition AFC03p268 and Founders Online. First printed, with normalised capitals, in Letters of Mrs. Adams, ed. Charles Francis Adams (1840)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A mother writing to a twelve-year-old gives the reader a use for the hard part of the day ahead: difficulty is where the habits of a strong mind get made.

candidates.quote: To work in silence and with all one’s heart, that is the writer’s lot; he is the only artist who must be a solitary, and yet needs the widest outlook upon the world.
candidates.author: Sarah Orne Jewett
candidates.locator: Letter to Willa Sibert Cather, 148 Charles Street, Boston, Sunday 13 December (1908), pp. 247 to 250, the sentence on p. 250; ed. Annie Fields (Houghton Mifflin, 1911); read in the archive.org scan lettersofsarahor00jewe
candidates.whyThisMonth: An older writer’s advice to Willa Cather, then buried in magazine work, names the practice exactly: quiet, the whole heart, and the hours alone that nobody sees.

candidates.quote: But I maintain that she would come if we worked for her, and that so to work, even in poverty and obscurity, is worth while.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.locator: Chapter 6, the closing sentence (Hogarth Press, 1929); read in the Project Gutenberg Australia text 0200791. She is Shakespeare’s sister, the poet who never wrote a word
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last sentence of the book makes unseen daily work its own justification: the labour counts even when nobody is watching and nothing comes of it yet.

candidates.quote: How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives.
candidates.author: Annie Dillard
candidates.locator: Chapter two (Harper and Row, 1989), p. 32, opening the paragraph on schedules; cited from memory of the book and its wide quotation, page to be confirmed by the verifier. A different line of hers, on workplaces, is shipped in the Makers year
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence the book is known by removes the gap between today and a life: what is done with this hour is the thing itself, so the hour is worth arranging.

candidates.quote: A beginner ought never to have a second arrow; for as long as he relies upon the other, he will be careless with his first one. At each shot he ought to think that he is bound to settle it with this particular shaft at any cost.
candidates.author: Yoshida Kenkō
candidates.work: Essays in Idleness (Tsurezuregusa), published in this translation as The Miscellany of a Japanese Priest
candidates.locator: Section 92, On the Waste of Time, pp. 74 to 75 (London: Humphrey Milford, 1914); read in the archive.org scan miscellanyofjapa00yosh. The section closes on how hard it is to do a thing at once, the instant one thinks of it. Donald Keene’s 1967 version of the same section is the better known English
candidates.speaker: the archery instructor, to his pupil
candidates.whyThisMonth: One of the best known sections of the book is a lesson against keeping a spare: treat this attempt, this morning, as the only arrow, and the carelessness goes out of it.

candidates.quote: I have suffered, like other writers, from indolence, irresolution, distaste to my work, absence of “inspiration,” and all that: but I have also found that sitting down, however reluctantly, with the pen in my hand, I have never worked for one quarter of an hour without finding myself in full train.
candidates.author: Harriet Martineau
candidates.locator: Volume I, Fourth Period, section I (1832, aged 30), p. 144 in the Boston edition (ed. Maria Weston Chapman; James R. Osgood, 1877; read in the fourth edition, Houghton, Osgood, 1879, archive.org scan cu31924104001791). Her sentence runs on after a colon (so that all the quarter hours, arguings, doubtings and hesitation … I now regard as so much waste); it is cut at the colon and given a full stop
candidates.whyThisMonth: The blurb’s own claim, practice not inspiration, from a woman who lived by her pen: fifteen minutes of sitting down to it, however unwillingly, and the mood arrives by itself.
